title: Shared ethics
hook: every stream teaches giving, kindness and justice

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: lay-led. A room where members take turns as the messenger of the congregation. What small job did you pick up? Today, what the streams hold in common when they act. Day one thousand two hundred forty-three.

Two families on the same street could argue for an hour about Shabbat, or prayer, or who counts in a minyan. One keeps every detail of Jewish law. The other keeps almost none. Yet on both kitchen windowsills sits the same small tin box with a slot in the lid. Coins go in before candles are lit on Friday, or when a child finds a quarter in the couch. The box doesn't argue. It just fills up. For a whole block we've walked through streams that differ. Today is about the ground they stand on together, and the box is a good place to start.
screen: `TWO FAMILIES, ONE ARGUMENT.` → `THE SAME TIN BOX.` → `THE BOX DOESN'T ARGUE.`

segments.voice: Shared ethics. Three words, and one ladder. First word: tzedakah, the giving that fills the box. It's usually translated charity, but some teachers hear in it tzedek, justice, and draw the lesson: giving is not a favor to the poor, it is part of setting the world right. Second word: chesed, kindness, the kind that goes beyond what anyone owes. An old teaching in the Mishnah, from Simeon the Just, says the world stands on three things: Torah, worship, and acts of loving-kindness. Third word: justice itself. The Torah doubles the word, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." And the prophet Micah gathers all three into one line: "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" Now the ladder. Maimonides, in his code of law, ranked ways of giving. Giving grudgingly sits low. Giving so that neither side knows the other sits high. And at the top he placed this: helping someone with a gift, a loan, a partnership or a job, so that they never need to ask again. Here's what makes this shared. These lines live in the Torah, the Prophets and the rabbinic books, the shelf the streams we have met read and argue over. Orthodox and Reform Jews may disagree about why a command binds. A Humanistic Jew may read Micah without a God who requires anything. The box on the windowsill still gets filled, and the soup still gets carried to the neighbor.
screen: `TZEDAKAH: GIVING AS JUSTICE.` · `CHESED: KINDNESS BEYOND WHAT'S OWED.` · `JUSTICE, JUSTICE SHALT THOU FOLLOW.` · `TOP OF THE LADDER: NO NEED TO ASK AGAIN.` · then, large: `SHARED ETHICS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something. Settle, and breathe. Let one person or one cause come to mind, someone who could use a little of what you have. Money is one way. Time is another. So is a skill: fixing, cooking, writing a letter for someone who can't. Choose one gift you can actually give today, small enough to do and real enough to matter. If you'd like, picture where it lands. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Shared ethics. Giving, kindness and justice: tzedakah, chesed and tzedek, taught from texts the streams hold in common, however they read them. Today's word.
Your line: shared ethics. Today, give the one thing you chose, and if you can, give it in a way that helps someone stand on their own. Day one thousand two hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Jewish homes and synagogues in different streams keep tzedakah boxes, collect for the poor before holidays, and run volunteer projects; giving is described as justice, not only generosity.
